text: Having a quantum error-correcting code is necessary, but not, by itself, sufficient. This lesson draws the line between having a QEC code and having a fault-tolerant architecture, precisely.

Every code in this course so far gives you a way to detect and correct errors on the data qubits once they've occurred. But a real quantum computation is a sequence of gates, measurements, and error-correction rounds, every one of which is itself a physical operation that can go wrong. Having a QEC code tells you how to fix an error — it doesn't by itself guarantee that fixing it won't introduce new errors faster than you can catch them. That's a genuinely different property from simply having a high enough code distance.

A fault-tolerant protocol ensures a single faulty component — one bad gate, one faulty ancilla, one bad measurement — does not propagate into a logical error the code can no longer correct. The emphasis is on containment: a single physical fault should, at worst, cause one correctable logical-level error, never an uncontrolled cascade. The building blocks are called gadgets — sub-circuits engineered so any single fault produces at worst a single correctable error on the output. Transversal gates, previewed with the Steane code, make this easy: since no qubit's gate operation touches another qubit during a transversal gate, a single faulty qubit's error can't spread within that operation. But not every needed gate can be made transversal, which sets up the next lesson.

Perhaps the most important and least obvious point: the syndrome-extraction circuits built in Chapters 3 and 5 are themselves physical circuits, made of real gates and measurements, subject to the exact same faults as everything else. A naively built extraction circuit could let a single faulty CNOT spread an error across multiple data qubits during the very process meant to detect and fix errors — self-defeating. Fault-tolerant syndrome extraction has to be designed, often using specially prepared, verified ancilla states, so this doesn't happen, which is why real architectures spend significant engineering effort on the error-correction circuitry itself.
Next lesson covers the one gate that resists the cheap transversal solution, and the expensive machinery — magic-state distillation — built to supply it anyway.
